title: How a SCUFFLE Decided the Browns' Most Important Battle of 2026
thumb_prompt: A football helmet lying on grass with torn chin strap after a training camp scuffle, with two offensive linemen in the background squaring up, dramatic late afternoon sunlight casting long shadows across practice field turf
thumb_subject: A determined rookie offensive tackle in an orange Browns practice jersey number fifty-five with sweat-drenched uniform

paragraphs.text: Sometimes in football, you earn your job not just with technique, but with heart. Spencer Fano learned that lesson Saturday when he got into a scuffle with Jared Verse, and by Monday, the ninth overall pick had locked down the starting left tackle job for the Cleveland Browns. This is not the way most people expected a first-round pick to cement his spot, but head coach Todd Monken made it official. Fano is done splitting reps with Dawand Jones. He is the guy. And it all came down to one moment when the rookie refused to back down against one of the league's most dangerous pass rushers.

Let's rewind to Saturday. The Browns are going through joint practice reps, and Fano is lined up against Verse, the two-time Pro Bowler Cleveland acquired in the Myles Garrett trade. Fano is holding his own. Then, after the whistle, things boil over. Verse rips Fano's helmet off and throws it to the side. The two hit the ground wrestling before coaches and teammates pull them apart. In most situations, that gets you benched or chewed out. Not this time. Monken loved it. On Monday, he praised Fano for not backing down, saying you want your left tackle to stand up for himself against a Pro Bowl rusher. That competitive fire sealed the deal.

This was not handed to Fano. Todd Monken has been adamant since Day One of camp that rookies have to earn their spots, no matter how high they were drafted. Dawand Jones started the first practice at left tackle, not Fano. The message was clear. Prove it. Over two weeks, Fano proved it. He showed the feet, the athleticism, the power. But Saturday was the moment where it all crystallized. Monken said you want to see your left tackle, the guy protecting your quarterback's blind side, not back down against elite competition. If Fano had wilted, if he had avoided Verse, that would have been a problem. Instead, he stood tall. And now he will be out there protecting whoever wins the quarterback job when the Browns open in Chicago.
card_lines: Fano won job over two weeks

paragraphs.text: Let's talk about the context here. Spencer Fano was not a slam dunk left tackle prospect. He has thirty-two and one-eighth inch arms, shorter than Will Campbell, the Patriots rookie who struggled in the Super Bowl. Pre-draft, there were questions about whether Fano would even play tackle or move inside to guard. He played right tackle his final two seasons at Utah, not left. But Andrew Berry and the Browns were confident. They traded down from six to nine, still landed Fano as the first offensive lineman off the board, and declared immediately that he would start at left tackle. That takes conviction. And now, Fano is proving them right. He won the Outland Trophy in college. He was a unanimous All-American. The talent was always there. The question was whether he could handle the left side and the speed of NFL edge rushers. Saturday, he answered that question.
card_lines: Played RT at Utah, not LT

paragraphs.text: Fano was not the only rookie promoted Monday. Denzel Boston, the second-round pick out of Washington, also earned first-team reps at wide receiver. And if you have been paying attention to camp reports, this should not be a surprise. Boston has been the star of training camp. Reporters are calling him the biggest winner of the first two weeks. He has been making contested catches, high-pointing the ball, drawing penalties because defensive backs cannot match his physicality. At six foot four and two hundred fifteen pounds, he gives the Browns a dimension they did not have last year. Jerry Jeudy and Cedric Tillman combined for just two touchdowns each in twenty twenty-five. Boston looks like he can change that.

The knock on Boston coming out of college was not talent. He had sixty-two catches for eight hundred eighty-one yards and eleven touchdowns as a junior. He was third-team All-Big Ten. The question was whether he could translate that size and catch radius to the NFL. So far, the answer is yes. Shedeur Sanders has connected with him on deep balls. Deshaun Watson hit him on a back-shoulder fade for a touchdown in eleven-on-eleven drills. Boston had what ESPN's Daniel Oyefusi called the catch of camp, leaping over a defensive back along the sideline to haul in a pass from Sanders in seven-on-seven. He is not just making routine plays. He is making the plays that change games. And he is doing it consistently.
card_lines: Best catch of camp vs. DBs

paragraphs.text: Here is what makes Boston's emergence so important. The Browns desperately need playmakers at wide receiver. Last year, their wide receivers combined for just four touchdowns. Four. In an entire season. Jerry Jeudy is a solid veteran, but he is not a guy who is going to dominate on contested catches or win jump balls in the red zone. Isaiah Bond is intriguing, but he is young. Cedric Tillman has battled injuries. KC Concepcion, the first-round pick, has flashed, but he also had a shoulder scare and has been inconsistent. Boston, meanwhile, has been steady. He has been the one constant in a wide receiver room that is still figuring itself out. If he can carry this into the preseason and regular season, the Browns offense suddenly has a real weapon.

Let's connect this to Browns history. Cleveland has struggled to develop wide receivers for years. They have hit on guys like Jarvis Landry and Amari Cooper in trades or free agency, but drafting and developing receivers has been a weak spot. Andrew Berry has not hit on a mid-round receiver yet. They have needed veterans to carry the load. Now, in the same draft, they took two receivers in the first two rounds, the highest Berry has ever used on the position in seven years. Concepcion went twenty-fourth overall. Boston went thirty-ninth. Both are flashing. If both hit, this could be the draft that changes the Browns offense for years. And right now, Boston looks like the safer bet to make an immediate impact. That is huge for a team that needs to find out if they have a quarterback worth building around.
card_lines: Berry's highest picks ever at WR

paragraphs.text: The Browns play their first preseason game Saturday in Chicago against the Bears. And now we know two key pieces of the offense. Spencer Fano will be protecting the blind side. Denzel Boston will be getting first-team reps at receiver. The one thing we still do not know? Who is starting at quarterback. Todd Monken said Monday the coaching staff would use Sunday to discuss who gets the start. It is either Deshaun Watson or Shedeur Sanders. Dillon Gabriel is in the mix too, but it feels like a two-man race. Watson has had an up-and-down camp, throwing six interceptions in the first four practices before bouncing back last week. Sanders has been more consistent, connecting with receivers on deep shots and showing poise in two-minute drills.

Here is the fascinating thing about this quarterback competition. It does not matter who starts Saturday in terms of the long-term plan. Monken has said each quarterback will start at least one preseason game. The Browns are going to evaluate all of them in real game action. But there is symbolic weight to who gets the first start. It tells you who is ahead right now. And if Sanders gets it, that is a huge statement about where this franchise is going. Watson is coming off multiple Achilles surgeries. He has not been good in Cleveland. The two hundred thirty million dollar contract looks like an albatross. Sanders was a fifth-round pick who fell on draft night. If he wins this job, it is one of the great redemption stories. And it gives the Browns hope that they found their guy without selling the farm.

Let's talk about what a Fano-Boston combination could mean for this offense. If Fano can protect the edge and give the quarterback time, and if Boston can win contested catches downfield, you suddenly have the foundation of a functional passing game. Add in KC Concepcion's speed, Jerry Jeudy's route running, and tight end Harold Fannin Jr., and there are weapons. The problem last year was not just the quarterback. It was that the offensive line could not protect, and the receivers could not separate or make contested plays. If Fano and Boston are real, those two problems start to get solved. Now, you still need a quarterback who can execute. That is the wildcard. But at least the Browns are putting pieces around whoever wins the job. That is progress.

There is a bigger picture here. The Browns are in year one of the Todd Monken era. Kevin Stefanski was not retained after the quarterback situation imploded last year. Monken, the former offensive coordinator, got promoted. Jim Schwartz, the defensive coordinator, resigned after being passed over. Mike Rutenberg is the new DC. Myles Garrett was traded to the Rams for Jared Verse and picks. This is a rebuild, whether the Browns want to call it that or not. And rebuilds are about finding young core pieces. Fano and Boston look like core pieces. Mason Graham, the first-round defensive tackle, has been a standout when healthy. If the Browns can hit on these draft picks, they have a foundation. If they whiff, this thing drags out another few years. So far, so good.

Spencer Fano grew up in Spanish Fork, Utah. He played at Timpview High School in Provo. He was a four-star recruit who committed to Utah and stayed in-state. As a freshman, he started at left tackle. Then the team needed him at right tackle, so he moved. He won the Outland Trophy in twenty twenty-five as the best interior lineman in college football. He was a unanimous All-American. He was the Polynesian College Football Player of the Year. He was first-team All-Big Twelve twice. And then on draft night, the Browns traded down from six to nine, still got him, and immediately said he would play left tackle again. Fano never blinked. He said he only moved in college because that is what the team needed. Now, the Browns need him at left tackle, and he is ready.
card_lines: Grew up in Spanish Fork, Utah

paragraphs.text: What makes Fano special is not his arm length. It is his feet and his athleticism. He has rare movement skills for a guy who is six foot six and three hundred fifteen pounds. He can mirror edge rushers. He can recover when he gets beat. He plays with an edge. That was clear Saturday when he did not back down from Verse. Fano said at his introductory press conference that he does not think anybody has the feet and athleticism he does, so the arm length does not matter. That is confidence. And so far, he is backing it up. The Browns took a calculated risk drafting a right tackle with short arms and declaring him their starting left tackle. If Fano pans out, Andrew Berry looks like a genius. If he struggles, it could set the offense back years. Right now, it looks like Berry nailed it.

Think about the left tackles the Browns have had over the years. Joe Thomas is the gold standard. Ten Pro Bowls. Hall of Famer. One of the best ever. After Thomas retired in twenty seventeen, it has been a carousel. Greg Robinson was a bust. Jedrick Wills was inconsistent and is now gone. The Browns have cycled through veterans and stopgaps. They have not had stability at the position since Thomas. Fano is supposed to change that. He is supposed to be the next franchise left tackle. That is a lot of pressure for a twenty-one-year-old rookie. But if Saturday was any indication, Fano is ready for it. He stood up to Jared Verse, a two-time Pro Bowler. He earned the respect of his head coach. And now, he has the job. The question is, can he keep it for the next decade like Joe Thomas did?

One more thing about Fano. He is part of a larger trend of the Browns betting on offensive linemen. They drafted Dawand Jones in the fourth round in twenty twenty-three. They traded for Tytus Howard from the Texans. They have Zion Johnson at guard. They have Elgton Jenkins at center. They released Jack Conklin and Wyatt Teller to clear cap space and committed to younger, cheaper options. The offensive line was a disaster last year. The Browns gave up the third-most sacks in the league. Deshaun Watson got destroyed. If you want to find out what you have at quarterback, you have to protect him. Fano is the centerpiece of that plan. If he and this line can hold up, the Browns offense has a chance. If not, it does not matter who the quarterback is. This all starts up front.

Here is what we learned this week. The Browns have two rookies who have earned starting jobs before the first preseason game. Spencer Fano at left tackle. Denzel Boston at wide receiver. Both were high picks. Both are delivering. And both give the Browns something they desperately needed: young, cost-controlled talent at key positions. In a league where rookie contracts are gold, hitting on your early-round picks is everything. The Browns have whiffed on plenty of drafts over the years. Baker Mayfield did not work out. Myles Garrett was traded. But if Fano and Boston hit, and if Mason Graham stays healthy, and if KC Concepcion develops, this twenty twenty-six draft class could be the foundation of the next good Browns team. That is the hope, anyway.

Saturday in Chicago, we will see how Fano and Boston look in real game action. Preseason game one does not count in the standings, but it matters for evaluation. The Browns need to see if Fano can handle NFL speed. They need to see if Boston can create separation and make plays against a real defense. They need to see which quarterback can move the ball. There are still a ton of questions about this team. The defense lost Myles Garrett and is under a new coordinator. The quarterback situation is a mess. The running back room is unproven. But at least at left tackle and wide receiver, the Browns have answers. That is progress. And in Cleveland, where progress has been rare, you take it where you can get it.

One final thought. The fact that a training camp scuffle decided a starting job tells you everything about Todd Monken's approach. He is not handing out jobs based on draft position. He is not coddling rookies. He is rewarding toughness, competitiveness, and performance. That is the culture he is trying to build. The Browns have been soft in recent years. They have been undisciplined. They have lacked an edge. Monken wants guys who will fight. Literally, in Fano's case. And that mentality, if it spreads through the roster, could change the identity of this team. The Browns are not going to out-talent the Ravens or the Bengals. But if they can out-tough people, if they can play with that Dawg Pound mentality, they have a chance. It starts with guys like Spencer Fano, who refused to back down.

So that is where we are. Eleven days until the preseason opener. Four days of camp left. Two rookies have locked down starting jobs. The quarterback battle rages on. The defense is adjusting to life without Myles Garrett. And the Browns are trying to figure out if they can compete in twenty twenty-six, or if this is truly a full rebuild. We will have a lot more answers after Saturday. But for now, the story is Spencer Fano and Denzel Boston. One won his job by fighting a Pro Bowler. The other won his job by dominating every day in camp. Both are exactly what the Browns needed. Let's see if it translates to game day. If it does, Cleveland might have something here. If it does not, well, there is always twenty twenty-seven.
